title: The early recording process and Bigard's first Ellington 'Bugle Call Rag'
summary: Early records used horns gathered in one bunch with no bass or drums, and he has never found his first Ellington record, 'Bugle Call Rag', from about January 1928.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Let's see, in 1927 you recorded with King Oliver --
-- and in 1928, Ellington, and then King Oliver again in 1928, right in the middle of your Ellington recording.

You know, I've been trying to find my first record that I made with Duke and nobody has it, and that's 'Bugle Call Rag.' I've been trying to locate it, and I know it's corny because each individual had a horn for himself to blow into and you couldn't use drums and you couldn't use bass because they wouldn't take on that recording. So you know that was a long time ago.
According to this January 1928. Is that about right?
What was the recording process used

then? Oh, it was -- they had individual horns that came into a gathering all in one bunch while this needle was going around this thing, and it was pretty hard to do because you didn't have any rhythm at all. It couldn't take the bass, it couldn't take drums.
